title: The Job We’re Actually Doing
author: Whitney Whealdon
summary: Whealdon borrows the Jobs To Be Done framework from product marketing and applies it to ELA instruction. Using the meal-kit example, she shows that people hire a product for the job their circumstances actually require, which is often not the advertised one. Teachers hire a curriculum to teach tested standards and produce evidence of mastery, not to deepen comprehension, because the system since No Child Left Behind rewards standards alignment. She argues that these are different jobs: students can master comprehension standards and still fail to comprehend complex texts, and standards-based test prep produces superficial comprehension and less desire to read. Drawing on her work at the Louisiana Department of Education, she describes redefining the job as helping all students read, understand, and express their understanding of complex grade-level texts, and leaving standards off the lessons. Her conclusion is that leaders must align the whole system (curriculum, assessment, data, professional learning, observation, incentives) around the real job rather than aligning teachers on process and compliance.
points: The Jobs To Be Done lens explains why teachers behave as they do: they organize their work around the job their circumstances reward, which is passing standards-based assessments, not the stated goal of comprehension.
Mastering comprehension standards and deeply comprehending complex texts are different jobs, and treating them as one leads to excerpts, test-mimic questions, and less reading.
Swapping in a new curriculum or tool changes nothing unless the surrounding systems (assessments, data reports, observations, incentives) support the job you actually want done.
Leaders can test any practice with one question: how does this help students read, understand, and express their understanding of complex grade-level texts?
Alignment should be on the shared job, not on process compliance such as pacing guides and trained-strategy checklists.
quotes: The story we have been selling to teachers for over 30 years is that by teaching students to master the standards, teachers are also improving students’ comprehension. The reality is, though, that these are different jobs.
Students can demonstrate mastery of comprehension standards and still not deeply comprehend complex texts. The implications of this are damning.

Instead of reading full-length texts, they focus on excerpts and give students questions that mimic what they will see on the state test. This answer-getting mentality often leads to less intellectual curiosity and less desire to read.

In our educational systems, aligning to standards is THE job to do. Once this immediate job dominates teacher behavior, all educational products and practices end up revolving around that job, not the job we say we want or think is important for students.

When the test results don’t look like what we want, we question whether teachers taught the standards well enough and suggest that teachers should work harder at doing that job. Why has no one questioned whether that is the right job?

But aligning the process does us no good if we haven’t aligned on the job. As the “Jobs To Be Done” framework reveals, people will organize their behavior around the job that helps them make progress within the circumstances they actually face.
This is what we did in Louisiana. Coherence came not from aligning processes, but from first getting everyone clear about the job we were trying to do and then aligning our systems around it.
